concepts.def: A change in the position of an organism, or of part of its body, brought about by the organism itself. Adaptations for movement are a universal feature of living organisms: motile organisms move the whole body from place to place (locomotion), while sessile organisms and plants move parts of the body, using mechanisms such as muscle contraction, the beating of cilia or flagella, differential growth or reversible changes in cell turgor.

A species whose individuals can move the whole body from place to place. Paramecium, a unicellular ciliate, swims by the coordinated beating of thousands of cilia; a fish or a cheetah moves by the contraction of skeletal muscle acting on a skeleton. Motility allows an organism to seek food, mates and favourable conditions and to escape from danger, and it is one of the two contrasting cases (motile and sessile) the guide asks students to explore.

A species whose adult individuals remain fixed in one place and do not move from place to place. The acorn barnacle, a crustacean, swims as a larva but cements itself to a rock as an adult; it still has adaptations for movement, using muscles to extend and beat its feathery cirri (modified legs) to sweep food from the water and to withdraw them and close its shell plates when disturbed. A sessile species shows that movement of body parts does not require locomotion.

The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril in striated muscle, extending from one Z line (Z disc) to the next. Thin actin filaments are anchored to the Z lines and thick myosin filaments occupy the centre, giving a dark A band (the full length of the myosin filaments), a light I band (actin only, on either side of a Z line) and a paler H zone in the middle of the A band (myosin only). During contraction the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide over one another: the A band keeps its width while the I band and H zone narrow.

The protein that forms the thin filaments of the sarcomere. Two chains of actin subunits twist around one another, and each subunit carries a site to which a myosin head can bind. In the relaxed sarcomere these sites are blocked by the regulatory protein tropomyosin, held in place by troponin; calcium ions binding to troponin move tropomyosin aside and expose the sites.

The motor protein that forms the thick filaments of the sarcomere. Each myosin molecule has a long tail, which bundles with other tails to form the filament, and a globular head that projects outwards. The head binds and hydrolyses ATP, attaches to actin to form a cross-bridge and pivots in the power stroke that pulls the actin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere.

The explanation of muscle contraction in which the actin and myosin filaments do not shorten but slide past one another, pulling the Z lines closer together and shortening the sarcomere. Sliding is driven by repeated cross-bridge cycles: a myosin head binds to actin, pivots in the power stroke (pulling actin towards the centre of the sarcomere and releasing ADP and phosphate), binds a new ATP (which detaches the head from actin), hydrolyses the ATP (which re-cocks the head) and attaches again further along the actin filament. Many heads cycling out of step generate a smooth pull.

concepts.term: Role of calcium ions in contraction
concepts.def: An action potential spreading over the membrane of a muscle fibre causes calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytoplasm around the myofibrils. Calcium ions bind to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin so that cross-bridges can form. When stimulation stops, calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by active transport, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again and the fibre relaxes.

An immense elastic protein, the largest known in humans, that runs from the Z line to the centre of the sarcomere (the M line) alongside the thick filaments and holds them in position. Titin acts as a molecular spring: when a sarcomere is stretched, titin is extended and stores potential energy, then recoils to return the sarcomere to its resting length when the stretching force is removed. Its resistance rises steeply as it is extended, so it also prevents the sarcomere from being overstretched to the point where the actin and myosin filaments no longer overlap.

A pair of muscles, or muscle groups, that produce opposite movements at a joint or in a body structure, such as the biceps and triceps at the elbow or the external and internal intercostal muscles of the ribcage. Muscle tissue can only exert force when it contracts, so a muscle cannot lengthen itself: it is stretched back to its resting length by contraction of its antagonist. When one member of the pair contracts, the other relaxes and is extended.

A single motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibres it stimulates. The axon of the motor neuron branches, forming a neuromuscular junction with each fibre, so when the neuron fires every fibre in the unit contracts together. A muscle contains many motor units; units in muscles used for fine movements, such as those moving the eye, contain few fibres, while units in large limb muscles may contain more than a thousand. The force of a contraction is graded by the number of motor units recruited and by the frequency of impulses.

The chemical synapse between the terminal of a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre. An action potential arriving at the terminal causes release of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft; acetylcholine binds to receptors on the membrane of the muscle fibre (the sarcolemma), depolarizing it and triggering an action potential that spreads over and into the fibre, causing release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and hence contraction.

A single elongated, multinucleate cell of skeletal muscle, formed during development by the fusion of many cells. It is packed with parallel myofibrils, each made of sarcomeres in series, and is surrounded by a membrane (the sarcolemma) and a network of sarcoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions. Each fibre is stimulated by one motor neuron at one neuromuscular junction, and belongs to one motor unit.

A hard external skeleton, found in arthropods such as insects and crustaceans, made of plates of chitin-containing cuticle joined by flexible regions at the joints. Muscles attach to the inner surface of the exoskeleton on either side of a joint, so contraction moves one section of the skeleton relative to another. The exoskeleton provides anchorage for muscles, acts as a system of levers and also protects and supports the body.

An internal skeleton of bone or cartilage, found in vertebrates. Muscles attach to the outer surface of bones by tendons, usually spanning a joint, so that when the muscle contracts one bone moves relative to another. The endoskeleton provides anchorage for muscles, acts as a system of levers, supports the body and grows with the animal.

A bone or exoskeletal plate acts as a rigid bar that pivots at a joint. In the lever the joint is the fulcrum, the force exerted by the contracting muscle where its tendon attaches is the effort, and the weight of the body part or object moved is the load. Because a muscle exerts force only by contracting and pulling, the lever converts a short, strong pull near the joint into a larger, faster movement at the far end of the bone, as when the biceps flexes the elbow.

A freely movable joint in which the ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage and enclosed in a capsule lined with a membrane that secretes synovial fluid. The human hip is a ball-and-socket synovial joint: the rounded head of the femur fits into a cup-shaped socket in the pelvis. Bones provide the rigid levers, cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock, synovial fluid lubricates the joint, ligaments hold the bones together, and muscles attached by tendons across the joint provide the force for movement.

A tough band of fibrous connective tissue that connects bone to bone across a joint. Ligaments hold the head of the femur in the socket of the pelvis, stabilize the hip joint and limit the range and direction of movement, helping to prevent dislocation. They are slightly elastic but do not contract.

A cord of tough, inelastic connective tissue that attaches a muscle to a bone. The tendon transmits the force of muscle contraction to the bone, so that muscles anchored on the pelvis and femur can move the hip joint. Tendons do not contract.

Smooth, slightly compressible connective tissue covering the articulating surfaces of the femur and pelvis at the hip joint. It reduces friction between the moving bones and absorbs shock during walking and running. It has no blood supply of its own and is nourished by the synovial fluid.

A viscous fluid secreted by the synovial membrane that lines the capsule of a synovial joint. It lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear on the cartilage, and supplies nutrients to the cartilage.

The extent of movement possible at a joint in a particular dimension, measured as the angle through which one bone can move relative to another from one extreme of the movement to the other. A joint's range of motion should be compared in several dimensions, for example flexion–extension, abduction–adduction and rotation at the hip: a ball-and-socket joint such as the hip moves through useful ranges in all three, while a hinge joint such as the knee moves mainly in one.

A protractor-like instrument with two arms and a pivot used to measure joint angles. The pivot is placed over the joint and the arms are aligned with the bones on either side; the angle is read at each extreme of the movement and the difference between the readings gives the range of motion. Joint angles can also be measured by computer analysis of photographs or video frames on which lines are drawn along the bones.

Two layers of muscle between adjacent ribs whose fibres run in opposite diagonal directions. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles pulls the ribcage up and outwards, increasing the volume of the thorax for inhalation; contraction of the internal intercostal muscles pulls the ribcage down and inwards for forced exhalation. The two layers are antagonistic: when one contracts it stretches the other, storing potential energy in the titin of the stretched sarcomeres. They are an example of antagonistic muscle action producing an internal body movement rather than locomotion.

Movement of a whole organism from one place to another. Locomotion is energetically costly, and animals locomote for reasons that increase survival or reproduction: foraging for food (a hummingbird flying between flowers for nectar), escaping from danger (a gazelle sprinting from a cheetah), searching for a mate (a male emperor moth flying upwind towards pheromone released by a female) and migration (the Arctic tern flying between Arctic breeding grounds and Antarctic waters each year).

Regular, usually seasonal, movement of animals between two regions, typically between breeding grounds and feeding or overwintering areas, followed by a return journey. Examples include the Arctic tern, which flies between the Arctic and the Antarctic each year; wildebeest, which move across the Serengeti following seasonal rains and fresh grazing; and humpback whales, which travel between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters. Migration is distinct from the one-way dispersal of young animals away from where they were born.

Locomotion in search of food. Examples include a hummingbird flying between flowers to drink nectar, a wolf pack travelling long distances to track prey and a honey bee flying between the hive and patches of flowers.

A smooth, tapered (fusiform) body shape that reduces drag as an animal moves through water. Marine mammals such as dolphins and whales are streamlined: the body is spindle-shaped, the hind limbs have been lost, external ears and genitals are absent or withdrawn into the body, hair is almost absent and a layer of blubber smooths the outline of the body.

A forelimb of a marine mammal modified for swimming. The flipper of a whale or dolphin contains the same bones as the forelimb of other mammals (humerus, radius, ulna and digits), but the bones are shortened and flattened and the whole limb is enclosed in a single paddle-shaped surface with no separate digits visible. In whales and dolphins the flippers are used for steering, braking and stability rather than for the main thrust.

The horizontal, boneless tail fin of a whale or dolphin, formed from tough connective tissue. The fluke is moved up and down by powerful muscles along the back and belly that flex the spine vertically, in contrast to the side-to-side beat of the vertical tail fin of a fish. The up-and-down stroke provides the thrust for swimming.

Marine mammals breathe air but spend most of their time submerged, so they breathe periodically: a series of rapid breaths at the surface, each exchanging a large proportion of the air in the lungs, separated by long dives during which they do not breathe. In whales and dolphins the nostrils have moved to the top of the head to form a blowhole, which is opened briefly at the surface and sealed shut by muscle while submerged, and the airway from the blowhole to the lungs is separated from the mouth and oesophagus, so that air is taken in only through the blowhole and food cannot enter the lungs.

mcqs.q: A student says: 'Adult barnacles are cemented to rocks and are sessile, so they are an exception to the idea that adaptations for movement are a universal feature of living organisms.' Which is the best response?
options: Barnacles are not an exception: the adult uses muscles to beat its feathery cirri to capture food and to close its shell plates when disturbed.
The student is right: once cemented to the rock the adult barnacle does not move at all, so it has no adaptations for movement.
The student is right: the adult barnacle is a passive filter feeder relying on the water current, so movement plays no part in its life.
The student is right: a barnacle has hard shell plates rather than a muscular system, and without muscle there can be no adaptation for movement.
mcqs.specStatementText: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
mcqs.explain: Adaptations for movement are universal. A sessile adult barnacle does not locomote, but it has muscles that move its cirri rhythmically to feed and that withdraw them and close the shell when it is disturbed. Movement of body parts is movement.
rationales: Adaptations for movement are universal. A sessile adult barnacle does not locomote, but it has muscles that move its cirri rhythmically to feed and that withdraw them and close the shell when it is disturbed. Movement of body parts is movement.

A student who equates sessile with motionless picks this. Sessile means the adult does not move from place to place; the barnacle still moves its cirri and shell plates by muscle contraction, so it has adaptations for movement.

A student who pictures a filter feeder as a sieve held in a current picks this. The barnacle actively extends and beats its cirri to sweep food from the water; the current does not do the work for it.

A student who equates movement with muscle picks this. The barnacle in fact has muscles that beat its cirri and close its shell plates; and even organisms without muscle, such as plants and ciliates, show movement by other mechanisms.

mcqs.q: Electron micrographs of a sarcomere are taken before and after it contracts. Which set of changes is observed?
options: The sarcomere is shorter; the A band, the I band and the H zone are all narrower, each in the same proportion.
The sarcomere is shorter; the A band keeps its width while the I band and the H zone are both narrower.
The sarcomere is shorter; the A band and the H zone keep their width and only the I band is narrower.
The sarcomere is shorter; the I band keeps its width while the A band and H zone are both narrower.
mcqs.explain: The filaments slide rather than shorten. The A band is the full length of the myosin filaments, so it is unchanged; the I band (actin only) and the H zone (myosin only) both narrow as the actin filaments slide further in over the myosin.
rationales: A student who thinks the filaments themselves shrink picks this. The myosin filaments keep their length, so the A band, which they define, keeps its width; only the regions of non-overlap narrow.

The filaments slide rather than shorten. The A band is the full length of the myosin filaments, so it is unchanged; the I band (actin only) and the H zone (myosin only) both narrow as the actin filaments slide further in over the myosin.

A student who applies 'the A band stays the same' to everything inside it picks this. The H zone is the part of the A band not overlapped by actin, so as overlap increases it narrows and can disappear.

A student who has swapped actin and myosin expects the band containing the thick filaments to keep its width but places those filaments in the I band. The thick myosin filaments define the A band, which is the one that keeps its width.

mcqs.q: What is the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction?
options: ATP is hydrolysed to power the pull of the head on actin; when ATP is used up the heads let go and the muscle relaxes.
One ATP is hydrolysed at the start of a contraction; the heads then ratchet along the actin without ever detaching.
Binding of ATP releases the myosin head from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the head for the next cycle.
ATP is not used by the myosin head; the power stroke is driven by calcium ions binding directly to it.
mcqs.explain: A myosin head bound to actin is released when a new ATP molecule binds to it. Hydrolysis of that ATP to ADP and phosphate returns the head to its cocked position, ready to attach further along the actin filament and carry out another power stroke.
rationales: A student who thinks ATP is only 'the energy for the pull' picks this. It is ATP binding that detaches the head from actin, so when ATP runs out the heads stay attached and the muscle locks, as in rigor mortis.
A student who pictures the heads walking along actin without letting go picks this. Each head must detach, re-cock and reattach many times during a contraction, and every cycle uses one ATP.

A myosin head bound to actin is released when a new ATP molecule binds to it. Hydrolysis of that ATP to ADP and phosphate returns the head to its cocked position, ready to attach further along the actin filament and carry out another power stroke.

A student who attaches the trigger to the mover picks this. Calcium ions bind to troponin on the thin filament, uncovering binding sites on actin; the energy for the cycle comes from ATP hydrolysed by the myosin head.

mcqs.q: A drug blocks the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of a skeletal muscle fibre. The motor neuron still stimulates the fibre normally. What is the effect on the fibre?
options: Myosin heads attach to actin but cannot pivot, because calcium ions are needed for the power stroke.
The fibre contracts normally, because the action potential in its membrane makes the filaments slide directly.
The fibre contracts normally, because calcium ions enter from the synaptic cleft, not from the reticulum.
No cross-bridges form, because tropomyosin still covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.
mcqs.explain: Without calcium ions, troponin does not change shape, tropomyosin is not moved and the myosin-binding sites on actin remain blocked. Myosin heads cannot attach, so there is no sliding and the fibre does not contract, even though it has been stimulated.
rationales: A student who thinks calcium acts on the myosin head picks this. Calcium ions act on troponin, controlling access to actin; the power stroke is driven by the myosin head using ATP, and it cannot happen because the heads never attach.

A student who treats calcium ions as a detail rather than a requirement picks this. The action potential does not act on the filaments; its only effect on contraction is to trigger release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the drug blocks that step, so the binding sites on actin stay covered.

A student who merges the two roles of calcium picks this. Calcium entering the neuron terminal triggers release of acetylcholine; the calcium that triggers sliding in a skeletal muscle fibre comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum inside the fibre.

Without calcium ions, troponin does not change shape, tropomyosin is not moved and the myosin-binding sites on actin remain blocked. Myosin heads cannot attach, so there is no sliding and the fibre does not contract, even though it has been stimulated.

mcqs.q: What are the roles of the protein titin in a sarcomere?
options: It acts as an elastic spring that returns a stretched sarcomere to its resting length and stiffens to stop it being overstretched.
It forms a third set of filaments that shorten actively to help pull the Z lines together during contraction.
It pulls a contracted sarcomere back out to its resting length, so that an antagonistic muscle is not required.
It is a rigid, inextensible cable from Z line to M line that stops the sarcomere from stretching at all.
mcqs.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
mcqs.explain: Titin runs from the Z line to the centre of the sarcomere. When the sarcomere is stretched, titin is extended and stores potential energy, then recoils; its resistance rises steeply near the limit of extension, so it also prevents overstretching.
rationales: Titin runs from the Z line to the centre of the sarcomere. When the sarcomere is stretched, titin is extended and stores potential energy, then recoils; its resistance rises steeply near the limit of extension, so it also prevents overstretching.

A student who assumes every sarcomere protein is contractile picks this. The force of contraction comes from myosin heads pulling on actin; titin is a passive elastic protein whose roles are in recoil and in limiting stretch.

A student who takes recoil to be the opposite of contraction picks this. Titin only recoils after it has been stretched; a sarcomere that has shortened by contraction can be lengthened only by an external force, such as an antagonistic muscle.

A student who hears 'prevents overstretching' as 'cannot stretch' picks this. Titin is elastic and extends readily over the normal range of sarcomere lengths; it only becomes very stiff near the limit of that range.

mcqs.q: The biceps contracts and shortens to flex the elbow. When the arm is then straightened, how is the biceps returned to its longer, resting length?
options: The biceps lengthens itself by reversing its cross-bridge cycle, so that the myosin heads push the actin filaments back outwards.
Contraction of the triceps moves the forearm, and this pulls the relaxed biceps longer, since a muscle cannot lengthen itself.
Titin in the biceps recoils and pulls its shortened sarcomeres back out, so the triceps is not needed for the movement.
The cross-bridges in the biceps release as its ATP is used up, and the limp muscle then falls back to its resting length on its own.
mcqs.specStatementText: Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
mcqs.explain: Muscle tissue exerts force only when it contracts. The triceps, the antagonist of the biceps, contracts to extend the elbow; the movement of the forearm stretches the relaxed biceps back to its resting length.
rationales: A student who thinks muscles can push as well as pull picks this. Cross-bridges only pull actin towards the centre of the sarcomere; there is no reverse power stroke, so a muscle cannot actively lengthen.

Muscle tissue exerts force only when it contracts. The triceps, the antagonist of the biceps, contracts to extend the elbow; the movement of the forearm stretches the relaxed biceps back to its resting length.

A student who takes titin recoil to be the general mechanism of relaxation picks this. Titin in a shortened sarcomere is slack, not stretched; it recoils only after the sarcomere has been pulled beyond its resting length.

A student who thinks relaxation is what happens when ATP runs out picks this. It is ATP binding that releases the heads, and a fibre without ATP locks rather than going limp; and even after the heads release, a shortened muscle stays short until an external force, the contracting triceps, pulls it longer.

mcqs.q: What is a motor unit in skeletal muscle?
options: One motor neuron and the single muscle fibre it contacts at one neuromuscular junction.
A whole muscle together with the single motor neuron that stimulates it to contract.
One motor neuron and all of the muscle fibres that its branching axon stimulates.
A muscle fibre fused to its motor neuron so that impulses pass straight into it.
mcqs.explain: The axon of a motor neuron branches to form a neuromuscular junction with each of many muscle fibres. The neuron and every fibre it supplies form one motor unit, and all of those fibres contract together when the neuron fires.
rationales: A student who has generalized from a diagram showing one axon terminal on one fibre picks this. A motor neuron forms junctions with many fibres, from a few to over a thousand, and all of them belong to its motor unit.
A student who remembers the single motor neuron of a reflex arc picks this. A muscle contains many motor units, each with its own motor neuron, and the number recruited sets the force of contraction.

The axon of a motor neuron branches to form a neuromuscular junction with each of many muscle fibres. The neuron and every fibre it supplies form one motor unit, and all of those fibres contract together when the neuron fires.
A student who imagines an electrical wiring picks this. The neuron and fibre are separate cells; the junction between them is a chemical synapse at which acetylcholine is released.

mcqs.q: In a study of two human muscles, a muscle that moves the eye (P) had about 20 000 fibres supplied by 2000 motor neurons, and a calf muscle (Q) had about 1 000 000 fibres supplied by 800 motor neurons. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: Q can be controlled more finely than P, because each of its motor neurons commands a far larger number of fibres.
P produces the more forceful contractions, because its greater number of neurons can send larger impulses.
Most of the fibres in Q cannot be stimulated, because a motor neuron can only form one neuromuscular junction.
Force can be increased in smaller steps in P than in Q, because its motor units contain fewer fibres.
mcqs.explain: Mean motor unit size is 20 000 / 2000 = 10 fibres in P and 1 000 000 / 800 = 1250 fibres in Q. Recruiting one more unit adds about 10 fibres of force in P but about 1250 in Q, so P can be controlled in much finer steps.
rationales: A student who equates bigger with better picks this. Large motor units give large increments of force, which suits a powerful calf muscle but not fine control; the small units of P allow smaller steps.

A student who thinks impulses vary in size picks this. Action potentials are all-or-nothing; force depends on the number of fibres recruited, and Q, with fifty times more fibres, can generate far more force.
A student who believes one neuron supplies one fibre picks this. The axon of a motor neuron branches to form a junction with every fibre in its unit, so 800 neurons can supply a million fibres.

Mean motor unit size is 20 000 / 2000 = 10 fibres in P and 1 000 000 / 800 = 1250 fibres in Q. Recruiting one more unit adds about 10 fibres of force in P but about 1250 in Q, so P can be controlled in much finer steps.

mcqs.q: A grasshopper's hind leg and a human leg both act as levers moved by muscles. Which comparison is correct?
options: In both, muscles anchored to a rigid skeleton pull across a joint; the grasshopper's attach inside its exoskeleton, the human's to the outside of bones.
In the grasshopper the muscles lie on the outside of the exoskeleton, the reverse of the human arrangement of muscles around bones.
Only the human leg is a true lever, because the grasshopper has no bones and its muscles move the leg without being anchored.
In both legs the contracting muscle acts as the fulcrum of the lever, while the joint supplies the effort that moves the load.
mcqs.specStatementText: Skeletons anchor muscles and act as levers
mcqs.explain: Exoskeleton and endoskeleton both provide anchorage for muscles and act as levers. Arthropod muscles attach to the inner surface of the cuticle on either side of a joint; vertebrate muscles attach by tendons to the outer surface of bones. In each case the joint is the fulcrum and the muscle pull is the effort.
rationales: Exoskeleton and endoskeleton both provide anchorage for muscles and act as levers. Arthropod muscles attach to the inner surface of the cuticle on either side of a joint; vertebrate muscles attach by tendons to the outer surface of bones. In each case the joint is the fulcrum and the muscle pull is the effort.

A student who extends 'exo' to everything picks this. The exoskeleton is outside the body, but the muscles are inside it, attached to its inner surface; the soft tissues are enclosed and protected by the cuticle.

A student who thinks muscles move limbs without anchorage picks this. A muscle must pull against a rigid part to produce movement; the grasshopper's cuticle plates are rigid and its leg is a lever, just as the human's is.

A student who has mapped the parts of a physics lever onto the wrong structures picks this. The joint is the fulcrum, the pull of the contracting muscle is the effort, and the weight of the leg and body is the load.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the roles of structures in the human hip joint?
options: Tendons join the pelvis to the femur and hold the joint together, and ligaments attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
Ligaments join the pelvis to the femur and stabilize the joint, and tendons attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
Cartilage covering the head of the femur secretes the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint and reduces friction.
The head of the femur rocks against the pelvis in a single plane, so the hip is a hinge joint like the knee.
mcqs.specStatementText: Inside a synovial joint: the hip
mcqs.explain: Ligaments are bone-to-bone connective tissue: they hold the head of the femur in the socket of the pelvis and limit movement to a safe range. Tendons are muscle-to-bone: they transmit the force of contraction to the femur and pelvis.
rationales: A student who has swapped the two kinds of connective tissue picks this. Ligaments connect bone to bone and stabilize the joint; tendons connect muscle to bone.

Ligaments are bone-to-bone connective tissue: they hold the head of the femur in the socket of the pelvis and limit movement to a safe range. Tendons are muscle-to-bone: they transmit the force of contraction to the femur and pelvis.

A student who assumes one friction-reducing structure makes the other picks this. Synovial fluid is secreted by the synovial membrane lining the joint capsule; the cartilage is a smooth covering that reduces friction and absorbs shock.

A student whose model of every joint is the knee or elbow picks this. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded head of the femur turns within the socket of the pelvis, allowing movement in three dimensions.

mcqs.q: A student measures the range of motion of the hip with a goniometer centred on the hip joint, one arm along the trunk and the other along the femur. With the thigh in line with the trunk the reading is 0°. The student flexes the hip as far as possible and records 125°, returns to 0°, then extends the hip backwards as far as possible and records 20°. What is the range of motion of the hip in the flexion–extension dimension?
mcqs.explain: Flexion and extension lie on opposite sides of the neutral position, so the thigh sweeps through 125° in front of the trunk plus 20° behind it: 125° + 20° = 145°.
rationales: A student who applies 'largest minus smallest' without picturing the movement picks this. The two extremes are on opposite sides of 0°, so the angles are added: 125° + 20° = 145°, not 125° − 20°.

A student who takes a single goniometer reading as the range picks this. 125° is the flexion angle only; the range of motion in this dimension includes the 20° of extension on the other side of the neutral position.
Flexion and extension lie on opposite sides of the neutral position, so the thigh sweeps through 125° in front of the trunk plus 20° behind it: 125° + 20° = 145°.
A student who assumes the hip moves equally far on both sides of neutral doubles the flexion reading. Extension was measured at only 20°, so the range is 125° + 20° = 145°.

mcqs.q: Joint angles measured by computer analysis of video images gave these ranges of motion for a volunteer. Hip: flexion 120°, extension 20°, abduction 45°, adduction 30°, medial rotation 40°, lateral rotation 45°. Knee: flexion 135°, extension 0°, abduction and adduction less than 5°, rotation less than 10°. Which conclusion do these data support?
options: The knee is the more mobile of the two joints, because its 135° flexion exceeds any single range at the hip.
Both joints are hinge joints, because in each the largest range measured lies in the flexion–extension dimension.
The range of motion of the hip in the flexion–extension dimension is 100°, the difference between 120° and 20°.
The hip moves through useful ranges in three dimensions, whereas the knee moves mainly in one.
mcqs.explain: The hip has substantial ranges in flexion–extension (140° in total), abduction–adduction (75°) and rotation (85°). The knee has a large range in flexion–extension only, with almost no movement in the other two dimensions, which is what a comparison across dimensions reveals.
rationales: A student who compares the single largest number picks this. Mobility of a joint is judged across dimensions: the knee moves in essentially one plane, the hip in three, so the hip is the more mobile joint.
A student who thinks every joint is a hinge picks this. A hinge joint moves in one plane only; the hip's 75° of abduction–adduction and 85° of rotation show that it is a ball-and-socket joint.
A student who subtracts the two readings picks this. Flexion and extension are measured on opposite sides of the neutral position, so the range in this dimension is 120° + 20° = 140°.

The hip has substantial ranges in flexion–extension (140° in total), abduction–adduction (75°) and rotation (85°). The knee has a large range in flexion–extension only, with almost no movement in the other two dimensions, which is what a comparison across dimensions reveals.

mcqs.q: During inhalation the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribcage up and outwards. What happens to the internal intercostal muscles at the same time, and why?
options: They are stretched, because their fibres run in the opposite direction, and the stretch stores potential energy in their titin.
They contract as well, because the internal intercostal muscles are the layer that moves the ribcage during inhalation.
They actively lengthen by pushing, so that the ribs are free to move; a muscle can exert force while lengthening.
They are stretched, and the energy of the stretch is stored as extra ATP in their fibres for the following exhalation.
mcqs.specStatementText: Intercostal muscles: antagonists working inside the body
mcqs.explain: The two layers are antagonistic. Because the fibres of the internal layer run in the opposite direction, the upward and outward movement of the ribs lengthens them; the extended titin in their sarcomeres stores potential energy that is released as they recoil when the external layer relaxes.
rationales: The two layers are antagonistic. Because the fibres of the internal layer run in the opposite direction, the upward and outward movement of the ribs lengthens them; the extended titin in their sarcomeres stores potential energy that is released as they recoil when the external layer relaxes.

A student who links 'internal' with 'inhale' picks this. The external intercostal muscles raise the ribcage for inhalation; the internal layer pulls it down and inwards during forced exhalation, and is stretched while the external layer contracts.
A student who thinks muscles can push picks this. Muscle tissue exerts force only when it contracts; the internal layer is lengthened passively by the movement produced by its antagonist.

A student for whom energy in muscle always means ATP picks this. Stretching does not synthesize ATP; the energy is stored as elastic potential energy in the extended titin molecules and released when they recoil.

mcqs.q: Which example of locomotion is correctly matched with its reason?
options: A young spider being carried away from its hatching site on a long thread of silk: migration.
A male emperor moth flying upwind along the trail of pheromone released by a female: searching for a mate.
A humpback whale swimming from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters where it does not feed: foraging for food.
A wildebeest herd crossing the Serengeti as seasonal rains and fresh grazing move: escaping from danger.
mcqs.explain: Male emperor moths detect the female's pheromone with their feathery antennae and fly upwind along the scent to reach her. The locomotion serves reproduction: it is a search for a mate.
rationales: A student who takes any movement away from home to be migration picks this. Ballooning spiderlings disperse in one direction and do not return; migration is a regular, usually seasonal, journey between regions and back.
Male emperor moths detect the female's pheromone with their feathery antennae and fly upwind along the scent to reach her. The locomotion serves reproduction: it is a search for a mate.

A student who assumes every journey is a search for food picks this. The whales leave the feeding grounds and do not feed in the breeding waters; the journey is migration, made for breeding and calving.

A student who sees herds as always fleeing predators picks this. The herd follows rainfall and grass growth in an annual circuit: this is migration. Escape from danger is a short, rapid response, such as a gazelle sprinting from a cheetah.

mcqs.q: How does the way a dolphin propels itself differ from the way a bony fish such as a tuna does?
options: Both tails beat from side to side; the dolphin's fluke is horizontal so that it can also act as a hydroplane.
The dolphin rows itself along with its flippers, while the tuna's thrust comes from its tail fin.
The dolphin's horizontal fluke beats up and down; the tuna's vertical tail fin beats from side to side.
The dolphin's flippers and fluke are fins of the same kind as the tuna's, so the two swim in the same way.
mcqs.explain: The fluke of a dolphin lies horizontally and is driven up and down by muscles that flex the spine vertically, as in a running land mammal. A fish's tail fin is vertical and is swept from side to side by muscles that flex the spine sideways.
rationales: A student who transfers the fish tail stroke to all swimmers picks this. A horizontal blade cannot push water backwards by moving sideways; the fluke beats up and down, which is the up-and-down movement named in the guide.
A student who thinks of the flippers as oars picks this. In dolphins and whales the flippers steer and stabilize; the thrust comes from the fluke, which is why the tail muscles are so large.

The fluke of a dolphin lies horizontally and is driven up and down by muscles that flex the spine vertically, as in a running land mammal. A fish's tail fin is vertical and is swept from side to side by muscles that flex the spine sideways.

A student who judges by outward shape picks this. The flipper is a modified forelimb with the bones of a mammalian limb, and the fluke is a boneless horizontal blade; the two animals move their tails in different planes.

mcqs.q: A sperm whale can stay submerged for over an hour, then breathes rapidly several times at the surface before diving again. Which adaptation of the airways makes this periodic breathing possible?
options: A blowhole on top of the head through which sea water taken in with food is forced out before each dive.
An airway that opens into the mouth as well as the blowhole, so that air can be taken in while the whale feeds.
Lungs that fill with sea water during the dive, so that dissolved oxygen is absorbed until the whale surfaces to empty them.
A blowhole on top of the head that is sealed shut while submerged and opened briefly at the surface.
mcqs.explain: The nostrils have moved to the top of the head to form the blowhole, so the whale can breathe with only a small part of its body above water. Muscles keep the blowhole sealed during the dive and open it briefly at the surface for each rapid exhalation and inhalation.
rationales: A student who thinks the spout is water from the mouth picks this. The blowhole is an airway, separate from the digestive system; the visible spout is exhaled air, moist and warm, condensing in cooler air.

A student who assumes whales breathe as humans do picks this. In whales the airway is separated from the mouth and oesophagus; air enters only through the blowhole, which keeps water out of the lungs during feeding.

A student who thinks a marine mammal can take oxygen from water while submerged picks this. Whales have no gills and their lungs hold only air; a long dive is possible because much of the lung air is exchanged in each rapid breath at the surface and oxygen is stored in blood and muscle.

The nostrils have moved to the top of the head to form the blowhole, so the whale can breathe with only a small part of its body above water. Muscles keep the blowhole sealed during the dive and open it briefly at the surface for each rapid exhalation and inhalation.

mcqs.q: Which set of features of a dolphin reduces drag as it swims, and so is an adaptation for streamlining?
options: A spindle-shaped body with the hind limbs lost, no external ears, almost no hair and an outline smoothed by a layer of blubber under the skin.
A thick layer of blubber that insulates the body; it makes the outline bulkier, but the extra drag is overcome by the powerful fluke.
A body made less dense by blubber and large lungs, so that the dolphin floats and does not have to push against the water as it swims.
Flippers and a fluke that are fins of the same kind as a fish's, replacing the limbs of a land mammal so that they cut through the water.
mcqs.explain: Streamlining is a fusiform body that lets water flow past with minimal turbulence. Loss of projecting structures (hind limbs, external ears, fur) and a layer of blubber that fills in the hollows of the body give the smooth, tapered outline that reduces drag.
rationales: Streamlining is a fusiform body that lets water flow past with minimal turbulence. Loss of projecting structures (hind limbs, external ears, fur) and a layer of blubber that fills in the hollows of the body give the smooth, tapered outline that reduces drag.
A student who knows blubber only as insulation picks this. Blubber fills in hollows and smooths the body outline, so it contributes to streamlining rather than adding drag.

A student who confuses drag with buoyancy picks this. Streamlining reduces the resistance of water to a moving body and is a matter of shape, not density; a floating body still has to push water aside to move.

A student who judges by outward shape picks this. The flippers are modified forelimbs containing mammalian limb bones and are used for steering, and the fluke provides thrust; drag is reduced by the shape of the whole body, not by fish-type fins.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B3.3 Muscle and motility

specStatements.text: Movement is universal, locomotion is not
Titin and antagonistic muscles in relaxation
Skeletons anchor muscles and act as levers
Inside a synovial joint: the hip
Intercostal muscles: antagonists working inside the body

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The hip joint is treated only in terms of the roles of bones, cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles and tendons, and the only bones students are asked to name are the femur and the pelvis. No item, concept or misconception requires the name of any hip muscle (such as the gluteal muscles or iliopsoas) or of any hip ligament. The 'not required' clause applies to the hip joint only. Where muscles of the elbow (biceps, triceps) are named under B3.3.3 and B3.3.5 (q06, m08, m23, c10, c16), they are supplied in the stem or in the options as context, and no item's key depends on the student recalling a muscle name; the biceps-triceps pair is the guide's standard illustration of antagonistic muscles.
